about: Every AArch32 instruction (A32 and T32, base, floating point, Advanced SIMD, crypto): what it does in our words, its forms and syntax, a link to Arm's page. The conditions are those of src/data/arm64-instructions.json.

source.forms: Arm AArch32 ISA XML for A-profile Architecture (developer.arm.com): mnemonics, form names, syntax templates, links
source.text: Descriptions written for this project; follow the links for the authoritative text

adc.description: Adds a register and a second operand (immediate, register optionally shifted or RRX, or in A32 a register shifted by a register) plus the carry flag. Compilers pair it with ADDS to add 64-bit integers held in two 32-bit registers: ADDS on the low words, ADC on the high words.

adcs.description: The flag-setting form of ADC: adds the operands and the carry, then updates N, Z, C and V. Used inside chains of additions wider than 64 bits; in Thumb the short 16-bit form outside an IT block always sets flags, so it is also printed where only the sum matters.
adcs.operation: Rd = Rn + op2 + C; NZCV = flags

add.description: Adds a register and an immediate, a register (optionally shifted, RRX or, in A32, shifted by a register) or the stack pointer. Compilers use it for arithmetic, address computation and adjusting sp (add sp, sp, #n in epilogues); an add from pc forms a PC-relative address and is printed as ADR.

adds.description: Adds like ADD and sets N, Z, C and V from the result. Compilers use it for overflow checks and for the low half of a 64-bit addition before ADC; Thumb code shows it often because the 16-bit add encodings outside an IT block always set flags.

addw.description: A Thumb-2 add of a plain 12-bit immediate (0–4095) to a register, sp or pc, for values that the usual rotated-constant form cannot express. Never sets flags; the pc form computes a PC-relative address like ADR.

adr.description: Puts into a register the address of a label near the current instruction, computed from pc (pc reads as the instruction address plus 8 in A32, plus 4 word-aligned in Thumb). Compilers use it in position-independent code for jump tables, literal data and nearby constants; it is the preferred name for ADD/SUB with pc.

aesd.description: Performs one AES decryption step on a 128-bit Q register: XOR with the round key in the other register, then the inverse ShiftRows and inverse SubBytes. Part of the ARMv8 Crypto extension available to 32-bit code; crypto libraries alternate it with AESIMC.

aese.description: Performs one AES encryption step on a 128-bit Q register: XOR with the round key in the other register, then ShiftRows and SubBytes. Part of the ARMv8 Crypto extension available to 32-bit code; crypto libraries alternate it with AESMC.

aesimc.description: Applies the AES InvMixColumns transform to a 128-bit Q register. Follows AESD in each decryption round except the last, and is also used to prepare the decryption key schedule.

aesmc.description: Applies the AES MixColumns transform to a 128-bit Q register. Follows AESE in each encryption round except the last; CPUs often fuse the pair into one operation.

and.description: Combines a register with an immediate or a (shifted) register using bitwise AND. Compilers use it to mask bits, test alignment and extract fields; does not touch the flags.

ands.description: Bitwise AND that also sets N and Z from the result and C from the shifter (V is left alone). Lets a mask and a following conditional branch share one instruction; frequent in Thumb, where the 16-bit form outside an IT block always sets flags.

asr.description: Shifts a register right by an immediate (1–32) or by the low byte of another register, copying the sign bit into the vacated bits. Compilers use it for signed division by powers of two and for sign extraction; it is a preferred name for MOV with an ASR shift.

asrs.description: Arithmetic shift right that also sets N and Z from the result and C from the last bit shifted out. Common in Thumb code, where the 16-bit shift encodings outside an IT block always set flags.

b.description: Jumps to a PC-relative label, either always or only when its condition suffix holds (beq, bne, blt…). Compilers use it for loops, if/else and tail calls; Thumb has short 16-bit forms and 32-bit .w forms with a range of about ±16 MB (±1 MB when conditional), A32 reaches ±32 MB.

bfc.description: Clears a run of width bits starting at bit lsb in a register, keeping all other bits. Compilers use it to zero bitfields in structures and to clear masks too wide for an immediate BIC.

bfi.description: Copies the low width bits of a source register into the destination starting at bit lsb, leaving the other bits of the destination unchanged. Compilers emit it for writes to C bitfields and for packing small values together.

bic.description: ANDs a register with the complement of an immediate or (shifted) register, clearing the bits that are set in the second operand. Compilers use it to clear flags in a word and to round values down to an alignment.

bics.description: The flag-setting form of BIC: clears the chosen bits and sets N and Z from the result and C from the shifter. Seen mainly in Thumb, where the 16-bit form outside an IT block always sets flags.

bkpt.description: Raises a debug breakpoint carrying an immediate that the debugger can read; it cannot be made conditional and runs even inside an IT block. Debuggers patch it into code to stop the program at a chosen place.

bl.description: Calls a function: saves the return address in lr (r14) and jumps to a PC-relative label, staying in the same instruction set (the Thumb return address has bit 0 set). The standard direct call; the range is about ±16 MB in Thumb and ±32 MB in A32, beyond that the linker inserts a veneer.

blx.description: Calls a function and may switch between A32 and Thumb: the label form always switches to the other instruction set, the register form jumps to the address in a register whose bit 0 selects Thumb. The register form is how compiled code calls through function pointers and virtual methods.
blx.operation: lr = return address; PC = target (bit 0 selects Thumb)

bx.description: Jumps to the address in a register, switching to Thumb when bit 0 is set and to A32 when it is clear. bx lr is the classic function return; it also serves indirect jumps and tail calls through pointers.

bxj.description: Once entered Jazelle Java bytecode execution when available; on current processors it behaves exactly like BX, jumping to a register address with bit 0 selecting Thumb. Practically never emitted by compilers.

cbnz.description: Thumb-only: jumps forward (up to 126 bytes) when a low register r0–r7 is not zero, without changing the flags. Compilers use it for short loop and null checks; it cannot appear inside an IT block.

cbz.description: Thumb-only: jumps forward (up to 126 bytes) when a low register r0–r7 is zero, without changing the flags. Typical for null-pointer checks and early exits; it cannot appear inside an IT block.

clrbhb.description: Clears the branch history the processor has gathered so that earlier code cannot steer the prediction of later indirect branches; a Spectre-BHB mitigation used by kernels. Sits in the hint space, so older CPUs run it as a NOP.

clrex.description: Drops the exclusive reservation set by a preceding LDREX, so that the next STREX fails. Used by kernels on context switches and by code that abandons an atomic retry loop.

clz.description: Counts the zero bits above the highest set bit of a register (32 for zero). Compilers emit it for __builtin_clz, integer logarithms, normalisation and software division.

cmn.description: Sets N, Z, C and V as if adding the second operand to a register, discarding the sum. Compilers use it to compare with a negative constant, for example cmn r0, #1 to test for -1.

cmp.description: Sets N, Z, C and V by subtracting an immediate or a (shifted) register from a register, discarding the difference. The usual instruction before a conditional branch, a conditional instruction or an IT block.

cps.description: Switches the processor to another mode (svc, irq, abt…) given as a number. Privileged: in user mode it has no effect. Found only in kernels, boot code and firmware.

cpsid.description: Masks the chosen interrupt kinds (a, i, f for asynchronous aborts, IRQ and FIQ), optionally also changing mode. Kernels use cpsid i to enter short critical sections; in user mode it does nothing.

cpsie.description: Unmasks the chosen interrupt kinds (a, i, f), optionally also changing mode. Pairs with CPSID at the end of a kernel critical section; in user mode it does nothing.

crc32b.description: Folds the low byte of a register into a running CRC-32 value using the IEEE 802.3 polynomial (as in zlib and Ethernet). An ARMv8 addition usable from 32-bit code; it cannot be conditional.

crc32cb.description: Folds the low byte of a register into a running CRC-32C value using the Castagnoli polynomial (as in iSCSI, ext4 and many storage formats). An ARMv8 addition usable from 32-bit code.

crc32ch.description: Folds the low 16 bits of a register into a running CRC-32C (Castagnoli) value. Used by checksum loops that handle a leftover halfword.

crc32cw.description: Folds a whole 32-bit register into a running CRC-32C (Castagnoli) value. The workhorse of hardware CRC-32C loops in 32-bit code.

crc32h.description: Folds the low 16 bits of a register into a running CRC-32 (IEEE polynomial) value. Used by checksum loops that handle a leftover halfword.

crc32w.description: Folds a whole 32-bit register into a running CRC-32 (IEEE polynomial) value. The main step of hardware CRC loops, for example in zlib built for ARMv8.

csdb.description: Stops later instructions from speculatively using results of conditional selects or moves whose condition is not yet resolved. A Spectre-v1 mitigation placed after bounds checks; on older CPUs it is a NOP.

dbg.description: Sends a numbered hint (0–15) to the debug and trace system; what it means depends on the implementation, and most CPUs treat it as a NOP. Rarely seen in compiled code.

dcps1.summary: Debug change PE state to EL1
dcps1.description: Thumb-only and valid only while an external debugger holds the processor in Debug state: moves it to EL1 (svc mode when EL1 is AArch32). Never part of a normal program.

dcps2.summary: Debug change PE state to EL2
dcps2.description: Thumb-only and valid only in Debug state under an external debugger: moves the processor to EL2 (Hyp mode when EL2 is AArch32). Never part of a normal program.

dcps3.summary: Debug change PE state to EL3
dcps3.description: Thumb-only and valid only in Debug state under an external debugger: moves the processor to EL3 (Monitor mode when EL3 is AArch32). Never part of a normal program.

dmb.description: Makes earlier memory accesses of the chosen kind observable before later ones (dmb ish for the inner shareable domain, ishst for stores only, sy for everything). On ARMv7 compilers surround atomic operations and LDREX/STREX loops with it to implement C++ and Java memory ordering.

dsb.description: Waits until all earlier memory accesses of the chosen kind, and cache and TLB maintenance, have completed before any later instruction runs. Stronger than DMB; used by kernels and drivers around device I/O and page table changes, and before WFI.

eor.description: XORs a register with an immediate or a (shifted) register. Compilers use it for toggling bits, hashing, checksums and sign tricks; it does not touch the flags.

eors.description: XOR that also sets N and Z from the result and C from the shifter. Common in Thumb code, where the 16-bit form outside an IT block always sets flags.

eret.description: Returns from an exception: in Hyp mode it restores pc from ELR_hyp and CPSR from SPSR_hyp; in other privileged modes it behaves like subs pc, lr, #0. Ends exception handlers in hypervisors and kernels.
eret.operation: PC = ELR_hyp or lr; CPSR = SPSR

esb.description: Makes pending SError (asynchronous RAS error) events synchronous at this point, possibly recording them in DISR. Used by kernels on exception entry; executes as a NOP without the RAS extension.

fldmdbx.summary: Load multiple D registers, old X format, decrement before
fldmdbx.description: A deprecated form of VLDMDB for 64-bit D registers that uses the old FSTMX transfer format with one extra unused word; the base register is decremented first and written back. Disassemblers print it when the word count in the encoding is odd; compilers no longer emit it.

fldmiax.summary: Load multiple D registers, old X format, increment after
fldmiax.description: A deprecated form of VLDMIA for 64-bit D registers that uses the old FSTMX transfer format with one extra unused word, optionally writing the advanced address back. Appears only when disassembling old VFP code or encodings with an odd word count.

fstmdbx.summary: Store multiple D registers, old X format, decrement before
fstmdbx.description: A deprecated form of VSTMDB (VPUSH) for 64-bit D registers that uses the old FSTMX format with one extra unused word; the base register is decremented first and written back. Printed for encodings with an odd word count; modern compilers do not emit it.

fstmiax.summary: Store multiple D registers, old X format, increment after
fstmiax.description: A deprecated form of VSTMIA for 64-bit D registers that uses the old FSTMX format with one extra unused word, optionally writing the advanced address back. Seen only in old VFP code or odd-count encodings.

hint.description: A hint-space encoding whose number has no name of its own, printed as hint #n. Processors that do not recognise the number execute it as a NOP; newer architecture versions may give it a meaning.

forms.heading: Hint with no name of its own

hlt.description: Stops the processor in Debug state for an external debugger when halting is enabled, otherwise it is undefined. Semihosting code for bare-metal targets uses it to call into the debugger.

hvc.description: Raises an exception taken to Hyp mode with a 16-bit immediate, letting a kernel call the hypervisor. Privileged and unconditional; seen in kernels, KVM and firmware, never in applications.

isb.description: Flushes the pipeline so that instructions after it are fetched again and see the effects of earlier system register changes, cache maintenance or code modification. Used by JIT compilers after writing code and by kernels after changing control registers.

it.description: Thumb-only prefix that makes the next one to four instructions conditional: the first runs if the condition holds, and each following T or E (as in itte eq) runs on the condition or its opposite. Compilers use it for short if/else and min/max sequences without branches; the instructions inside print their condition suffix.
it.operation: next 1–4 instructions run if cond (T) or !cond (E)

lda.description: Loads a 32-bit word from the address in a register with acquire ordering: no later memory access can be observed before it. ARMv8 code uses it for C++ atomic loads with acquire or seq_cst ordering instead of LDR followed by DMB.

ldab.description: Loads a byte with acquire ordering and zero-extends it to 32 bits. ARMv8 code uses it for acquire loads of atomic bools and chars.

ldaex.description: Loads a word with acquire ordering and marks the address for exclusive access. ARMv8 code begins atomic read-modify-write and compare-and-swap loops with it, ending them with STLEX or STREX.

ldaexb.description: Loads a byte with acquire ordering, zero-extends it and marks the address for exclusive access. Starts atomic loops on 8-bit values, finished by STLEXB or STREXB.

ldaexd.description: Loads 64 bits into a pair of registers with acquire ordering and marks the address for exclusive access. Used for 64-bit atomics (std::atomic<int64_t>) in 32-bit ARMv8 code, together with STLEXD.

ldaexh.description: Loads a halfword with acquire ordering, zero-extends it and marks the address for exclusive access. Starts atomic loops on 16-bit values, finished by STLEXH or STREXH.

ldah.description: Loads a halfword with acquire ordering and zero-extends it to 32 bits. ARMv8 code uses it for acquire loads of 16-bit atomics.

ldc.description: Originally a load into a coprocessor; in ARMv8 the only remaining form loads a word from memory into the debug communications register DBGDTRTXint (p14, c5), with offset, pre- or post-indexed addressing or a PC-relative label. Seen only in debug monitor code.

ldm.description: Loads a list of registers from consecutive words starting at the base address, optionally writing the advanced address back (!). With sp! it is printed as POP; loading pc makes it a return, as in pop {r4, r7, pc}. The A32 forms with ^ restore user-mode registers or return from an exception.

ldmda.description: A32-only: loads a list of registers from consecutive words ending at the base address (the lowest at Rn - 4n + 4), optionally lowering the base by 4n. Rare in compiled code; LDMFA is its name in full-ascending stack notation.

ldmdb.description: Loads a list of registers from the words just below the base address (Rn - 4n up to Rn - 4), optionally lowering the base by 4n. Old A32 frame-pointer epilogues used it, as in ldmdb r11, {r4, r11, sp, pc}; LDMEA is another name for it.

ldmea.description: Another name for LDMDB in the 'empty ascending' stack notation: pops registers from a stack that grows upward with the base pointing at the next free word. Disassemblers print LDMDB instead.

ldmed.description: Another name for LDMIB in the 'empty descending' stack notation: pops registers from a downward-growing stack whose pointer addresses the next free word. A32-only; disassemblers print LDMIB instead.

ldmfa.description: Another name for LDMDA in the 'full ascending' stack notation: pops registers from an upward-growing stack whose pointer addresses the last used word. A32-only; disassemblers print LDMDA instead.

ldmfd.description: Another name for LDM (LDMIA) in the 'full descending' stack notation, the stack model of the Arm ABI: with sp! it is exactly POP. Disassemblers print LDM or POP instead.

ldmib.description: A32-only: loads a list of registers from the words just above the base address (Rn + 4 up to Rn + 4n), optionally raising the base by 4n. Rare in compiled code; LDMED is another name for it.

ldr.description: Loads a 32-bit word using an immediate or (shifted) register offset, with optional pre-index (!) or post-index writeback, or from a PC-relative literal pool. The most common load: variables, spills, constants, addresses; loading pc is a jump (PLT stubs, jump tables), and ldr Rt, [sp], #4 prints as POP.

ldrb.description: Loads a byte from memory and zero-extends it to 32 bits, with the same immediate, register, pre/post-index and literal forms as LDR. Compilers use it for unsigned char, bool and byte-wise string processing.

ldrbt.description: Loads a byte and zero-extends it, performing the access with user-mode permissions even when running privileged. Kernels use it when reading user memory; A32 has post-indexed forms, Thumb an offset form.

ldrd.description: Loads two 32-bit registers from consecutive words, with immediate or (A32) register offset, pre/post-index or a literal. Compilers use it for 64-bit integers and soft-float doubles; A32 needs an even first register followed by its neighbour, Thumb accepts any pair.

ldrex.description: Loads a word and marks the address for exclusive access, so that a later STREX succeeds only if nobody wrote there in between. The basis of atomics on ARMv7: compilers build atomic add, exchange and compare-and-swap as LDREX/STREX retry loops, usually between DMB barriers.

ldrexb.description: Loads a byte, zero-extends it and marks the address for exclusive access. Starts atomic loops on 8-bit values such as std::atomic<bool>, finished by STREXB.

ldrexd.description: Loads 64 bits into two registers and marks the address for exclusive access. The only way ARMv7 code can read a 64-bit value atomically; paired with STREXD for 64-bit atomic updates (A32 needs an even/odd register pair).

ldrexh.description: Loads a halfword, zero-extends it and marks the address for exclusive access. Starts atomic loops on 16-bit values, finished by STREXH.

ldrh.description: Loads a 16-bit halfword and zero-extends it, with immediate or register offset, pre/post-index or literal forms (A32 register offsets cannot be shifted). Compilers use it for unsigned short, char16_t and UTF-16 strings.

ldrht.description: Loads a halfword and zero-extends it with user-mode access permissions even when running privileged. Used by kernels to read user memory safely.

ldrsb.description: Loads a byte and sign-extends it to 32 bits, with immediate, register, pre/post-index and literal forms. Compilers use it for signed char and int8_t values.

ldrsbt.description: Loads a byte and sign-extends it, with user-mode access permissions even when running privileged. Used by kernels reading user memory.

ldrsh.description: Loads a halfword and sign-extends it to 32 bits, with immediate, register, pre/post-index and literal forms. Compilers use it for short and int16_t, for example 16-bit audio samples.

ldrsht.description: Loads a halfword and sign-extends it, with user-mode access permissions even when running privileged. Used by kernels reading user memory.

ldrt.description: Loads a word with user-mode access permissions even when running privileged, so a kernel copying from user space gets a fault on addresses the user may not read. A32 has post-indexed immediate and register forms, Thumb an offset form.

lsl.description: Shifts a register left by an immediate (0–31) or by the low byte of another register (32 or more gives zero), filling with zeros. Compilers use it for multiplication by powers of two, array indexing and building bit masks; a preferred name for MOV with an LSL shift.

lsls.description: Logical shift left that also sets N and Z from the result and C from the last bit shifted out. Very common in Thumb code, where the 16-bit shift outside an IT block always sets flags; also used to move a bit into C or N for a following branch.

lsr.description: Shifts a register right by an immediate (1–32) or by the low byte of another register, filling with zeros. Compilers use it for unsigned division by powers of two and for extracting high bits; a preferred name for MOV with an LSR shift.

lsrs.description: Logical shift right that also sets N and Z from the result and C from the last bit shifted out. Common in Thumb, where the 16-bit form outside an IT block always sets flags; lsrs by 1 moves the lowest bit into C.

mcr.description: Writes a general register to a coprocessor register selected by coproc, opc1, CRn, CRm and opc2; on ARMv7/v8 these are the p15 and p14 system registers. Kernels use it for cache, TLB and MMU control; old user code used mcr p15, 0, rX, c7, c10, 5 as a memory barrier.

mcrr.summary: Move to coprocessor from two registers
mcrr.description: Writes a pair of general registers to a 64-bit coprocessor register, such as the LPAE translation table bases or the generic timer compare values. Found in kernels and hypervisors.

mla.description: Multiplies two registers and adds a third, keeping the low 32 bits (the same for signed and unsigned). Compilers use it for a*b+c, array index arithmetic and dot products.

mlas.description: A32-only flag-setting form of MLA: computes Ra + Rn * Rm and sets N and Z from the result, leaving C and V unchanged. Rare in compiled code.
mlas.operation: Rd = Ra + Rn * Rm; NZ = flags

mls.description: Multiplies two registers and subtracts the product from a third, keeping the low 32 bits. Compilers emit it for c - a*b and for the remainder after a division: a - (a / b) * b.

mov.description: Copies an immediate or a register, possibly shifted, into a register; LLVM prints the shifted forms as ASR, LSL, LSR, ROR or RRX. The 16-bit immediate form (movw) loads 0–65535. Compilers use it for copies between registers and small constants; mov pc, lr is an old-style return.

movs.description: Copies an immediate or (shifted) register and sets N and Z from the value and C from the shifter. Very common in Thumb, where movs r0, #imm is the short 16-bit way to load a small constant; in privileged A32 code movs pc, lr returns from an exception.

movt.description: Writes a 16-bit immediate into the upper half of a register, keeping the lower half. Paired with MOVW to build any 32-bit constant or symbol address in two instructions (movw r0, #:lower16:sym; movt r0, #:upper16:sym).

movw.description: Loads a 16-bit immediate (0–65535) into a register, clearing the upper half. Compilers use it for constants that do not fit a rotated immediate and, together with MOVT, for full 32-bit constants and addresses.

mrc.description: Reads a coprocessor register (p15 or p14 system registers on ARMv7/v8) into a general register. Android's bionic reads the thread pointer with mrc p15, 0, rX, c13, c0, 3 (TPIDRURO) for thread-local storage; kernels read ID, fault and control registers.

mrrc.summary: Move to two registers from coprocessor
mrrc.description: Reads a 64-bit coprocessor register into a pair of general registers. The vDSO's clock_gettime reads the virtual counter with mrrc p15, 1, rX, rY, c14 (CNTVCT); kernels use it for LPAE translation table bases.

mrs.description: Copies a status register into a general register: APSR (the N, Z, C, V, Q and GE flags) in user code, CPSR or SPSR in privileged code, or with the banked form a register of another mode. Used to save flags or interrupt state.

msr.description: Writes a register or (A32 only) an immediate into chosen fields of APSR, CPSR or SPSR, or with the banked form into a register of another mode. User code can only change the flags (APSR_nzcvq, APSR_g); kernels use it to switch modes and restore interrupt state.

mul.description: Multiplies two registers and keeps the low 32 bits of the product, which are the same for signed and unsigned operands. Compilers use it for every 32-bit integer multiplication by a non-constant value.

muls.description: Multiplies like MUL and sets N and Z from the result, leaving C and V unchanged. Usually seen in Thumb, where the 16-bit multiply outside an IT block always sets flags.

mvn.description: Writes the bitwise complement of an immediate or a (shifted) register. Compilers use it for ~x and to load constants whose complement is easy to encode, for example mvn r0, #0 for -1.

mvns.description: The flag-setting form of MVN: writes the complement and sets N and Z from it and C from the shifter. Seen mostly in Thumb, where the 16-bit form outside an IT block always sets flags.

nop.description: Does nothing and changes no state. Compilers and linkers use it as padding to align loops and functions (nop.w in Thumb fills four bytes).

orn.description: Thumb-only: ORs a register with the complement of an immediate or (shifted) register. Compilers use it for x | ~y and to set many bits with a constant that is easier to encode inverted.

orns.description: Thumb-only flag-setting form of ORN: computes Rn | ~op2 and sets N and Z from the result and C from the shifter.

orr.description: ORs a register with an immediate or a (shifted) register. Compilers use it to set bits and flags, combine bitfields and, with a shifted operand, to join two halves of a value.

orrs.description: OR that also sets N and Z from the result and C from the shifter. Compilers use orrs on the two halves of a 64-bit value to test it for zero; common in Thumb, where the 16-bit form outside an IT block always sets flags.

pkhbt.description: Builds a register from the bottom halfword of one register and the top halfword of another, optionally shifted left first. Used in DSP and media code to pack two 16-bit values before parallel arithmetic.

pkhtb.description: Builds a register from the top halfword of one register and the bottom halfword of another, optionally shifted arithmetically right first. Used in DSP and media code to pack 16-bit results.

pld.description: Hints that data at an address (base plus immediate or shifted register, or a literal) will soon be read, so the cache can fetch it early. Has no architectural effect and never faults; compilers emit it for __builtin_prefetch and in memcpy-style loops.

pldw.description: Hints that data at an address will soon be written, letting the cache fetch the line in a writable state. Part of the multiprocessing extensions; seen in memset-style loops and lock code.

pli.description: Hints that code at an address will soon be executed, so the instruction cache can fetch it early. Has no architectural effect; rare in compiled code.

pop.description: Loads a list of registers from the stack at sp and raises sp past them; another name for LDMIA sp! (or LDR Rt, [sp], #4 for one register). Function epilogues use it, and popping into pc (pop {r4-r7, pc}) returns, switching to Thumb or Arm by bit 0 of the loaded address.

pssbb.description: Stops later loads from speculatively bypassing earlier stores to the same physical address. A Spectre-style mitigation placed by hand or by hardened compilers; it never changes the result of correct code.

push.description: Lowers sp and stores a list of registers there, lowest register at the lowest address; another name for STMDB sp! (or STR Rt, [sp, #-4]! for one register). Function prologues use it to save callee-saved registers and lr, as in push {r4-r7, lr}.

qadd.description: Adds two signed 32-bit registers, clamping the result to the int32 range instead of wrapping, and sets the sticky Q flag when it clamps. Met in DSP and codec code and behind the ACLE __qadd intrinsic.

qadd16.description: Adds the two signed 16-bit halves of one register to those of another, clamping each sum to the int16 range. Unlike QADD it leaves the Q flag alone. Hand-tuned audio and video code uses it to process two samples at once.

qadd8.description: Adds the four signed bytes of one register to those of another, clamping each sum to -128..127. The Q and GE flags are not touched. Used in hand-written pixel and signal processing loops.

qasx.summary: Saturating add and subtract with exchange
qasx.description: Swaps the halfwords of the second operand, then adds in the top half and subtracts in the bottom half, clamping both signed 16-bit results. Handy for complex-number arithmetic on packed 16-bit pairs; flags are not changed.

qdadd.description: Doubles the second operand with saturation, then adds it to the first with saturation, setting the Q flag if either step clamps. Fixed-point (Q31) DSP code uses it to accumulate products that need a shift by one.

qdsub.description: Doubles the second operand with saturation, then subtracts it from the first with saturation, setting the Q flag if either step clamps. The subtracting partner of QDADD in Q31 fixed-point code.

qsax.summary: Saturating subtract and add with exchange
qsax.description: Swaps the halfwords of the second operand, then subtracts in the top half and adds in the bottom half, clamping both signed 16-bit results. The mirror image of QASX; flags are not changed.

qsub.description: Subtracts one signed 32-bit register from another, clamping the result to the int32 range and setting the sticky Q flag when it clamps. Found in DSP code and behind the ACLE __qsub intrinsic.

qsub16.description: Subtracts the two signed 16-bit halves of one register from those of another, clamping each difference to the int16 range. The Q and GE flags are left as they are.

qsub8.description: Subtracts the four signed bytes of one register from those of another, clamping each difference to -128..127. No flags change. Used in hand-written byte-wise image and signal code.

rbit.description: Reverses the order of all 32 bits of a register. Compilers pair it with CLZ to count trailing zeros (__builtin_ctz), since AArch32 has no direct instruction for that.

rev.description: Reverses the order of the four bytes of a register, converting between little-endian and big-endian. Compilers use it for __builtin_bswap32, htonl/ntohl and reading big-endian file formats.

rev16.description: Swaps the two bytes inside each 16-bit half of a register independently. Used for htons-style conversions and for byte-swapping pairs of 16-bit values.
rev16.operation: Rd = bswap16 of each halfword of Rm

revsh.description: Swaps the two bytes of the low halfword and sign-extends the result to 32 bits. Compilers use it to byte-swap a signed 16-bit value such as an int16_t read from a big-endian stream.

rfe.description: Loads a return address and a saved status word from memory at Rn (increment-after by default), branches to the address and restores the CPSR from the word, optionally writing back Rn. Kernel exception handlers use it together with SRS; it never appears in Android user code.

rfeda.description: The RFE variant that reads the two words ending at Rn: the return address from Rn - 4 and the status word from Rn, restoring the CPSR and branching. Arm state only; kernel code.

rfedb.description: The RFE variant that reads the two words just below Rn: the return address from Rn - 8 and the status word from Rn - 4, restoring the CPSR and branching. Used by kernel exception exit paths.

rfeea.description: Another name for RFEDB in the 'empty ascending' stack notation: it pops the return address and saved status from a stack that grows upward with sp pointing at the next free slot.

rfeed.description: Another name for RFEIB in the 'empty descending' stack notation: it pops the return address and saved status from a downward-growing stack whose pointer sits on the next free slot.

rfefa.description: Another name for RFEDA in the 'full ascending' stack notation: it pops the return address and saved status from an upward-growing stack whose pointer sits on the last used slot.

rfefd.description: Another name for RFEIA (plain RFE) in the 'full descending' stack notation, the usual stack layout: it pops the return address and saved status pushed earlier by SRSDB.

rfeib.description: The RFE variant that reads the two words just above Rn: the return address from Rn + 4 and the status word from Rn + 8, restoring the CPSR and branching. Arm state only; kernel code.

ror.description: Rotates a register right by an immediate or by the low byte of another register; bits leaving the bottom re-enter at the top. In Arm state it is MOV with a rotated operand; compilers emit it for rotate idioms in hashes and ciphers.

rors.description: Like ROR, but also sets N and Z from the result and C from the last bit rotated out. The 16-bit Thumb form outside an IT block always sets flags, so Thumb code often shows RORS where only the rotation matters.

rrx.description: Shifts a register right by one bit and fills the top bit from the carry flag, a 33-bit rotation through C. Compilers use it after LSRS on the high word to shift a 64-bit value right by one.

rrxs.summary: Rotate right with extend, setting flags
rrxs.description: Like RRX, shifting the carry into the top bit, but also moves the bit shifted out of the bottom into C and sets N and Z. Lets multi-word right shifts by one carry on through several registers.

rsb.description: Subtracts a register from the second operand (an immediate, a register or a shifted register), the reverse of SUB. Compilers use rsb Rd, Rn, #0 to negate and forms like rsb Rd, Rn, Rn, lsl #3 to multiply by 7.

rsbs.description: Like RSB, but sets NZCV from the result. Negating a 64-bit value uses RSBS on the low word followed by RSC or SBC on the high word; Thumb also shows it as the 16-bit negate (the NEGS form).

rsc.description: Subtracts a register and the borrow (inverted carry) from the second operand. Arm state only; it finishes multi-word reverse subtraction, such as negating a 64-bit value after RSBS.

rscs.summary: Reverse subtract with carry, setting flags
rscs.description: Like RSC, but also sets NZCV, so the borrow can feed further words of a multi-word reverse subtraction. Arm state only.

sadd16.description: Adds the two signed 16-bit halves of one register to those of another, wrapping on overflow, and sets the GE flags of each half when its sum is not negative. A following SEL can use those GE bits to pick results per half.
sadd16.operation: Rd.h[i] = Rn.h[i] + Rm.h[i]; GE from each sum

sadd8.description: Adds the four signed bytes of one register to those of another, wrapping, and sets one GE flag per byte when that sum is not negative. Hand-written byte-wise code pairs it with SEL for branch-free per-byte choices.

sasx.description: Swaps the halfwords of the second operand, then adds in the top half and subtracts in the bottom half as signed 16-bit values, wrapping, and sets the GE flags of each half from its result. Useful for packed complex-number arithmetic.
sasx.operation: Rd.h[1] = Rn.h[1] + Rm.h[0]; Rd.h[0] = Rn.h[0] - Rm.h[1]; GE set

sb.description: Prevents the CPU from speculatively executing later instructions until earlier ones are resolved. A Spectre mitigation, placed after bounds checks by hardened code; it does not change program results.

sbc.description: Subtracts the second operand (immediate, register or shifted register) and the borrow, the inverted carry flag, from a register. Compilers use it for the high word of 64-bit subtraction after SUBS on the low word.

sbcs.description: Like SBC, but also sets NZCV from the result. Compilers use it in 64-bit comparisons (SUBS then SBCS, followed by a signed or unsigned condition) and in subtraction chains longer than two words.

sbfx.description: Copies a run of bits from a register to the bottom of the destination and sign-extends it to 32 bits. Compilers use it to read signed struct bitfields and for sign-extending odd-width values.

sdiv.description: Divides one signed 32-bit register by another, rounding toward zero; dividing by zero gives 0. Hardware division is optional in ARMv7-A, so armeabi-v7a code usually calls __aeabi_idiv instead and emits SDIV only when built for a CPU that has it.

sel.description: Builds the result byte by byte, taking each byte from the first operand when its GE flag is set and from the second otherwise. Follows a parallel add or subtract (SADD8, USUB8…) to implement per-byte max, min or clamping without branches.

setend.description: Switches the byte order used by data loads and stores to big-endian (BE) or little-endian (LE) for the current thread. Deprecated since Armv8; old hand-written code used it around blocks of big-endian data.

setpan.description: Turns the PAN bit on or off; while it is on, privileged code faults when touching user memory. The kernel uses it around user-copy routines; in user mode it does nothing.

sev.description: A hint that sets the event register of every core, waking those waiting in WFE. Spinlock release code issues it after storing the unlocked value.

sevl.description: A hint that sets the event register of the current core only, so the first WFE in a following wait loop falls straight through. Armv8 spin-wait loops start with it.

sha1c.description: Performs four SHA-1 rounds with the choose function on the hash state in a Q register, using the e value and four schedule words from the other operands. Part of the Armv8 crypto extension, used by BoringSSL and OpenSSL.

sha1h.description: Rotates the low 32-bit element left by 30 places, the step that derives the next e value in SHA-1, and clears the rest of the destination. Crypto extension.

sha1m.description: Performs four SHA-1 rounds with the majority function on the hash state in a Q register, using the e value and four schedule words from the other operands. Used for rounds 40–59 of SHA-1.

sha1p.description: Performs four SHA-1 rounds with the parity function on the hash state in a Q register, using the e value and four schedule words from the other operands. Used for rounds 20–39 and 60–79 of SHA-1.

sha1su0.description: First half of computing the next four SHA-1 message schedule words from earlier ones held in three Q registers; SHA1SU1 completes it.

sha1su1.description: Second half of computing the next four SHA-1 message schedule words, finishing what SHA1SU0 began. Crypto extension, used by SHA-1 code in TLS libraries.

sha256h.description: Performs four SHA-256 rounds and produces the updated first half (a–d) of the hash state, taking the other half and four schedule words plus constants from the other Q registers.

sha256h2.description: Performs the same four SHA-256 rounds as SHA256H but produces the updated second half (e–h) of the hash state; the two are issued as a pair.

sha256su0.description: First half of computing the next four SHA-256 message schedule words from earlier ones; SHA256SU1 completes it. Crypto extension.

sha256su1.description: Second half of computing the next four SHA-256 message schedule words, finishing what SHA256SU0 began.

shadd16.description: Adds the signed 16-bit halves of two registers and halves each sum, so the result never overflows. Averaging two packed samples is the typical use; flags are not changed.

shadd8.description: Adds the four signed bytes of two registers and halves each sum, keeping every result in range. Flags are not changed.

shasx.summary: Halving add and subtract with exchange
shasx.description: Swaps the halfwords of the second operand, adds in the top half and subtracts in the bottom half as signed values, then halves both results so they cannot overflow. Flags are not changed.

shsax.summary: Halving subtract and add with exchange
shsax.description: Swaps the halfwords of the second operand, subtracts in the top half and adds in the bottom half as signed values, then halves both results. The mirror image of SHASX; flags are not changed.

shsub16.description: Subtracts the signed 16-bit halves of one register from those of another and halves each difference, so the result never overflows. Flags are not changed.

shsub8.description: Subtracts the four signed bytes of one register from those of another and halves each difference. Flags are not changed.

smc.description: Raises an exception into the secure monitor (Monitor mode or EL3 firmware); the 4-bit immediate is ignored by the hardware. Kernels use it to request firmware services such as PSCI power management; user code cannot execute it.

smlabb.description: Multiplies the signed low halfwords of two registers and adds the 32-bit product to an accumulator, setting the Q flag if the addition overflows (the result still wraps). Compilers emit it for multiply-adds of int16_t values.

smlabt.description: Multiplies the signed low halfword of the first register by the signed high halfword of the second and adds the product to an accumulator, setting Q if the addition overflows. Saves an extra shift when 16-bit values are packed in pairs.

smlad.summary: Dual 16-bit multiply, add both to accumulator
smlad.description: Multiplies the matching signed halfwords of two registers (low by low, high by high) and adds both products to an accumulator, setting Q if the sum overflows. A dot-product step for packed 16-bit samples in filters and codecs.
smlad.operation: Rd = Ra + Rn.h[0] * Rm.h[0] + Rn.h[1] * Rm.h[1]

smladx.summary: Dual 16-bit multiply crosswise, add to accumulator
smladx.description: Like SMLAD, but swaps the halfwords of the second operand first, multiplying low by high and high by low, then adds both products to the accumulator; Q is set on overflow. Used in complex multiply-accumulate.
smladx.operation: Rd = Ra + Rn.h[0] * Rm.h[1] + Rn.h[1] * Rm.h[0]

smlal.description: Multiplies two signed 32-bit registers and adds the 64-bit product to the 64-bit value held in the RdLo/RdHi pair. Compilers emit it for int64_t sums of 32-bit products, common in fixed-point and audio code.

smlalbb.description: Multiplies the signed low halfwords of two registers and adds the product to the 64-bit accumulator in RdLo/RdHi, which cannot overflow in practice. For long sums of 16-bit products.

smlalbt.description: Multiplies the signed low halfword of the first register by the high halfword of the second and adds the product to the 64-bit accumulator in RdLo/RdHi.

smlald.description: Multiplies the matching signed halfwords of two registers and adds both products to the 64-bit accumulator in RdLo/RdHi. The long version of SMLAD for dot products that would overflow 32 bits.

smlaldx.description: Like SMLALD, but swaps the halfwords of the second operand first, so it multiplies low by high and high by low before adding both products to the 64-bit accumulator.

smlals.description: Like SMLAL, adding a signed 64-bit product to RdHi:RdLo, but also sets N and Z from the 64-bit result. Arm state only and rarely produced by compilers.

smlaltb.description: Multiplies the signed high halfword of the first register by the low halfword of the second and adds the product to the 64-bit accumulator in RdLo/RdHi.

smlaltt.description: Multiplies the signed high halfwords of two registers and adds the product to the 64-bit accumulator in RdLo/RdHi.

smlatb.description: Multiplies the signed high halfword of the first register by the signed low halfword of the second and adds the product to an accumulator, setting Q if the addition overflows.

smlatt.description: Multiplies the signed high halfwords of two registers and adds the product to an accumulator, setting Q if the addition overflows. Compilers use it when both int16_t operands come from the upper half, e.g. after a load of a packed pair.

smlawb.description: Multiplies a signed 32-bit register by the signed low halfword of another, keeps the top 32 bits of the 48-bit product and adds an accumulator, setting Q on overflow. Fixed-point (Q31 × Q15) DSP code uses it.

smlawt.description: Multiplies a signed 32-bit register by the signed high halfword of another, keeps the top 32 bits of the 48-bit product and adds an accumulator, setting Q on overflow.

smlsd.description: Multiplies the matching signed halfwords of two registers, subtracts the high product from the low one and adds the difference to an accumulator, setting Q if that addition overflows. The real-part step of packed complex multiplication.
smlsd.operation: Rd = Ra + Rn.h[0] * Rm.h[0] - Rn.h[1] * Rm.h[1]

smlsdx.description: Like SMLSD, but swaps the halfwords of the second operand first, so the products are low × high and high × low; their difference is added to the accumulator, with Q set on overflow.
smlsdx.operation: Rd = Ra + Rn.h[0] * Rm.h[1] - Rn.h[1] * Rm.h[0]

smlsld.description: Multiplies the matching signed halfwords of two registers, subtracts the high product from the low one and adds the difference to the 64-bit accumulator in RdLo/RdHi.

smlsldx.summary: Dual crosswise multiply, subtract, long accumulate
smlsldx.description: Like SMLSLD, but swaps the halfwords of the second operand first, so the products are low × high and high × low; their difference goes into the 64-bit accumulator in RdLo/RdHi.

smmla.description: Multiplies two signed 32-bit registers, takes the high 32 bits of the 64-bit product (truncated) and adds an accumulator. Fixed-point Q31 code uses it for multiply-adds that need only the upper word.

smmlar.description: Like SMMLA, but rounds instead of truncating: it adds the accumulator shifted into the top word and 0x80000000 to the 64-bit product before keeping the high 32 bits.

smmls.description: Subtracts the signed 64-bit product of two registers from the accumulator placed in the top word, and keeps the high 32 bits of the result (truncated).

smmlsr.description: Like SMMLS, but adds 0x80000000 before keeping the high 32 bits, so the result is rounded rather than truncated.

smmul.description: Multiplies two signed 32-bit registers and returns the high 32 bits of the 64-bit product. Compilers use it for signed division by a constant (multiplying by a magic number) and for Q31 fixed-point multiplication.

smmulr.description: Like SMMUL, but adds 0x80000000 to the 64-bit product before taking the high 32 bits, rounding to nearest. Used for rounded Q31 fixed-point multiplication.

smuad.description: Multiplies the matching signed halfwords of two registers and adds the two products, setting Q if the sum overflows (only when all four halves are -32768). A two-element dot product of packed 16-bit data.

smuadx.description: Like SMUAD, but swaps the halfwords of the second operand first, adding low × high and high × low products; Q is set on overflow. Gives the imaginary part of a packed complex multiplication.

smulbb.description: Multiplies the signed low halfwords of two registers into a full 32-bit product. Compilers emit it for multiplying two int16_t values, avoiding separate sign extensions.

smulbt.description: Multiplies the signed low halfword of the first register by the signed high halfword of the second into a 32-bit product.

smull.description: Multiplies two signed 32-bit registers and writes the full 64-bit product to the RdLo/RdHi pair. Compilers use it for int64_t results of 32-bit multiplication and for signed division by constants.

smulls.description: Like SMULL, writing the signed 64-bit product to RdHi:RdLo, but also sets N and Z from that result. Arm state only and seldom seen in compiled code.

smultb.description: Multiplies the signed high halfword of the first register by the signed low halfword of the second into a 32-bit product. Saves a shift when one operand sits in the upper half.

smultt.description: Multiplies the signed high halfwords of two registers into a 32-bit product, e.g. after x >> 16 on both operands.

smulwb.description: Multiplies a signed 32-bit register by the signed low halfword of another and keeps the top 32 bits of the 48-bit product. Fixed-point Q31 × Q15 code, such as audio filters, uses it.

smulwt.description: Multiplies a signed 32-bit register by the signed high halfword of another and keeps the top 32 bits of the 48-bit product.

smusd.description: Multiplies the matching signed halfwords of two registers and subtracts the high product from the low one; the difference cannot overflow, so no flag changes. Gives the real part of a packed complex multiplication.

smusdx.description: Like SMUSD, but swaps the halfwords of the second operand first, so it computes low × high minus high × low. No flags change.

srs.description: Stores lr and the SPSR of the current mode onto the stack of another processor mode, chosen by number, at increasing addresses from that mode's sp, optionally updating it. Kernel exception entry code uses it to save state for a later RFE; never seen in Android user code.

srsda.description: The SRS variant that writes lr and the SPSR to the two words ending at the chosen mode's sp. Arm state only; also called SRSED in the 'empty descending' stack notation.

srsdb.description: The SRS variant that writes lr and the SPSR just below the chosen mode's sp, the usual full descending push (also called SRSFD). Kernel exception entry paths use it, pairing with RFEIA on the way out.

srsib.description: The SRS variant that writes lr and the SPSR just above the chosen mode's sp. Arm state only; also called SRSFA in the 'full ascending' stack notation.

ssat.description: Optionally shifts a register (LSL or ASR), then clamps it to the range of a signed integer of 1 to 32 bits, setting the Q flag if it had to clamp. Compilers emit it for clamps such as min(max(x, -128), 127).

ssat16.description: Clamps each signed 16-bit half of a register to the range of a signed integer of 1 to 16 bits, setting the Q flag if either half was clamped. Used when narrowing packed 16-bit samples.

ssax.description: Swaps the halfwords of the second operand, then subtracts in the top half and adds in the bottom half as signed 16-bit values, wrapping, and sets the GE flags of each half from its result. The mirror image of SASX.
ssax.operation: Rd.h[1] = Rn.h[1] - Rm.h[0]; Rd.h[0] = Rn.h[0] + Rm.h[1]; GE set

ssbb.description: Stops later loads from speculatively reading stale data by bypassing earlier stores to the same virtual address. A Spectre variant 4 mitigation; it does not change program results.

ssub16.description: Subtracts the two signed 16-bit halves of one register from those of another, wrapping, and sets the GE flags of each half when its difference is not negative. A following SEL can then pick per-half maxima or minima.
ssub16.operation: Rd.h[i] = Rn.h[i] - Rm.h[i]; GE from each difference

ssub8.description: Subtracts the four signed bytes of one register from those of another, wrapping, and sets one GE flag per byte when that difference is not negative. Paired with SEL for branch-free per-byte comparisons.

stc.description: Stores data from a coprocessor to memory at a base register plus offset, with offset, pre-index, post-index or unindexed addressing. In Armv8 only the p14, c5 form remains, which writes the debug data-transfer register; compiled Android code does not use it.

stl.description: Stores a 32-bit register with release ordering, so all earlier memory accesses become visible first. Armv8 AArch32 code uses it for C11 release and seq_cst atomic stores and lock release; ARMv7 code uses DMB plus STR instead.

stlb.description: Stores the low byte of a register with release ordering. Used for atomic stores to bool or uint8_t variables with release or seq_cst order in Armv8 code.

stlex.description: Stores a word with release ordering only if the core still holds the exclusive reservation from a load-exclusive; writes 0 to Rd on success and 1 on failure. It closes the retry loop of compare-and-swap and atomic read-modify-write code.

stlexb.description: Exclusive store of the low byte of a register with release ordering; Rd gets 0 on success and 1 on failure. The byte-sized partner of LDAEXB in atomic loops.

stlexd.description: Exclusively stores two registers as one 64-bit value with release ordering; Rd gets 0 on success and 1 on failure. Compilers use it with LDAEXD for 64-bit atomics such as std::atomic<int64_t>.
stlexd.operation: if exclusive: [Rn] = Rt, Rt2; Rd = status (release)

stlexh.description: Exclusive store of the low halfword of a register with release ordering; Rd gets 0 on success and 1 on failure. Used with LDAEXH for 16-bit atomic operations.

stlh.description: Stores the low halfword of a register with release ordering. Used for atomic stores to 16-bit variables with release or seq_cst order in Armv8 code.

stm.description: Stores a list of registers to consecutive words starting at the base register, lowest register first, optionally advancing the base past them (Rn!); STMIA and STMEA are other names. Compilers use it with LDM to copy small structs and blocks; the ^ form, privileged only, stores user-mode registers.

stmda.description: Stores a list of registers to the words ending at the base register, so the highest register lands at Rn, optionally lowering the base by the size of the block. Arm state only; STMED is the same in stack notation and compilers rarely emit it.

stmdb.description: Stores a list of registers to the words just below the base register, optionally lowering the base by the size of the block. With sp! as base it is exactly PUSH (STMFD in stack notation); otherwise it fills buffers from the top.

stmea.description: Another name for STMIA in the 'empty ascending' stack notation: stores a list of registers to consecutive words going up from the address in Rn, and with ! writes the end address back. Disassemblers print stm or stmia instead.

stmed.description: Another name for STMDA in the 'empty descending' stack notation (A32 only): stores a list of registers so that the highest one lands at the address in Rn and the rest go below it; with ! Rn drops by the block size. Disassemblers print stmda.

stmfa.description: Another name for STMIB in the 'full ascending' stack notation (A32 only): stores a list of registers to consecutive words starting 4 bytes above Rn; with ! Rn grows by the block size. Disassemblers print stmib.

stmfd.summary: Store multiple, full descending (= STMDB, PUSH)
stmfd.description: Another name for STMDB in the 'full descending' notation of the usual Arm stack: stores registers in the words just below the address in Rn. With sp and writeback it is a push, and that is how disassemblers show it; otherwise they print stmdb.

stmib.description: Stores a list of registers to consecutive words starting 4 bytes above the address in Rn (A32 only), the lowest-numbered register at the lowest address; with ! Rn moves past the stored block. Rare in compiled code, which prefers stm (increment after) and push.

str.description: Stores a 32-bit register to memory at a base register plus an immediate or a (shifted) register offset, with pre-indexed (! writeback) and post-indexed forms; str rX, [sp, #-4]! pushes a single register. Compilers use it for every word-sized store to locals, globals and fields.

strb.description: Stores the low 8 bits of a register to memory, with the same addressing as STR: immediate or register offset, pre- and post-indexed. Compilers use it for char, bool and uint8_t stores and in byte-by-byte copy loops.

strbt.description: Stores the low byte of a register with the permission checks of user mode, even when the code runs privileged; A32 forms are post-indexed, the Thumb form takes a small positive offset. Only kernels use it to write into user memory; app code never does.

strd.description: Stores two registers to eight consecutive bytes, the first at the lower address. A32 needs an even register followed by the next one (r0/r1, r2/r3…) and also allows a register offset; Thumb takes any two registers with an immediate offset. Compilers use it for 64-bit values and to save register pairs.

strex.description: The store half of an LDREX/STREX pair: writes Rt to [Rn] only if the exclusive monitor set by the matching LDREX is still held, and puts 0 (success) or 1 (failure) into Rd. Compilers loop on it to build atomic read-modify-write and compare-and-swap on armv7.

strexb.description: Stores the low byte of Rt to [Rn] only if the exclusive monitor from a matching LDREXB is still held, reporting 0 (success) or 1 (failure) in Rd. Compilers use the pair for atomic operations on 8-bit values such as std::atomic<bool> or atomic<char>.

strexd.description: Stores two registers as one 64-bit value to [Rn] only if the exclusive monitor from a matching LDREXD is still held, reporting 0 or 1 in Rd. Together with LDREXD it is how armv7 performs 64-bit atomics; in A32 Rt must be even and Rt2 the next register.

strexh.description: Stores the low 16 bits of Rt to [Rn] only if the exclusive monitor from a matching LDREXH is still held, reporting 0 (success) or 1 (failure) in Rd. Compilers use the pair for atomic operations on 16-bit values such as std::atomic<short>.

strh.description: Stores the low 16 bits of a register to memory at a base plus an immediate or register offset, with pre- and post-indexed forms (A32 allows no shift on the offset register). Compilers use it for short, uint16_t and char16_t stores.

strht.description: Stores the low halfword of a register with the permission checks of user mode, even when the code runs privileged; A32 forms are post-indexed, the Thumb form takes a small positive offset. Meant for kernels writing to user memory; app code does not use it.

strt.description: Stores a 32-bit register with the permission checks of user mode, even when the code runs privileged; A32 forms are post-indexed with an immediate or register offset, the Thumb form takes a small positive offset. Only kernels use it, to write into user memory safely.

sub.description: Subtracts the second operand (an immediate, a register optionally shifted by a constant or, in A32, by a register) from Rn and writes Rd without touching the flags. sub sp, sp, #n allocates stack space in prologues; sub Rd, pc, #n is the ADR form for addresses before the instruction.

subs.description: Subtracts like SUB and also sets N, Z, C and V (C = 1 when no borrow occurs). Used for loop counters counted down to zero and subtractions that feed a condition; 16-bit Thumb forms outside an IT block always set flags. subs pc, lr, #n returns from an exception.
subs.operation: Rd = Rn - op2; NZCV = flags(Rn - op2)

subw.description: The Thumb-2 form of SUB that takes a plain 12-bit immediate from 0 to 4095 instead of a rotated constant, and never sets flags. Compilers use it for stack adjustments and pointer offsets that the modified-constant encoding cannot express.

svc.description: Raises a supervisor-call exception so the operating system kernel takes over. On Android and Linux the immediate is 0, the system call number travels in r7, arguments in r0–r6 and the result comes back in r0; libc's syscall wrappers are where you meet it.

sxtab.description: Takes the low byte of Rm (optionally rotated right by 8, 16 or 24 first), sign-extends it to 32 bits and adds it to Rn. Compilers fold a signed char or int8_t widening into an addition or address calculation with it.

sxtab16.summary: Sign-extend two bytes and add halfwords
sxtab16.description: Picks bytes 0 and 2 of Rm (after an optional rotation by 8, 16 or 24), sign-extends each to 16 bits and adds them to the two halfwords of Rn separately. DSP and codec code uses it to unpack signed 8-bit samples into 16-bit lanes.

sxtah.description: Sign-extends the low halfword of Rm (optionally rotated right by 8, 16 or 24 first) to 32 bits and adds it to Rn. Compilers use it to fold a short-to-int conversion into an addition or an address calculation.

sxtb.description: Sign-extends the low 8 bits of Rm (optionally after rotating it right by 8, 16 or 24) to 32 bits. Compilers emit it when a signed char or int8_t value is widened to int, for example after a byte load or before a comparison.

sxtb16.description: Sign-extends bytes 0 and 2 of Rm (after an optional rotation by 8, 16 or 24) into the two 16-bit halves of Rd. DSP code uses it, often twice with rotations 0 and 8, to unpack signed 8-bit values into halfword lanes for the parallel 16-bit instructions.

sxth.description: Sign-extends the low 16 bits of Rm (optionally after rotating it right by 8, 16 or 24) to 32 bits. Compilers emit it when a short or int16_t value is widened to int.

tbb.description: Branches forward by twice the unsigned byte read from [Rn + Rm]; Rn is usually pc, so the byte table sits right after the instruction. Thumb-2 compilers use it for dense switch statements whose cases lie within 510 bytes.

tbh.description: Branches forward by twice the unsigned halfword read from [Rn + Rm*2]; with Rn = pc the table of 16-bit offsets follows the instruction. Thumb-2 compilers use it for switch statements too large for TBB, reaching up to about 128 KB ahead.

teq.description: Computes Rn XOR the second operand, discards the result and sets N and Z from it (C from the shifter for shifted operands; V unchanged). Compilers use it to test two values for equality without disturbing the carry, or to check whether two signs differ.

trap.description: How LLVM prints the permanently undefined encoding compilers emit for __builtin_trap: the Thumb halfword 0xdefe (udf #254) or the A32 word 0xe7ffdefe. It always raises an undefined-instruction exception, which Android reports as SIGILL; you find it after failed checks and in unreachable code.

tsb.description: Ensures that trace data generated by earlier instructions is flushed before later ones run, for self-hosted tracing (Armv8.4). It lives in the hint space, so older CPUs execute it as a nop; application code does not use it.

tst.description: ANDs Rn with the second operand, discards the result and sets N and Z (C from the shifter when the operand is shifted; V unchanged). Compilers use it to check flag bits or alignment, as in tst r0, #1 followed by a conditional branch or an IT block.

uadd16.description: Adds the two unsigned 16-bit halves of Rn and Rm separately, wrapping around, and sets each pair of GE bits when its halfword sum carried out. Hand-written DSP code uses it for two-lane 16-bit arithmetic; the GE bits can then drive SEL.

uadd8.description: Adds the four unsigned bytes of Rn and Rm lane by lane, wrapping around, and sets a GE bit for each byte whose sum carried out. Optimized strlen and memchr add 0xFF to every byte so the GE bits mark the non-zero ones, then use SEL.

uasx.summary: Unsigned add and subtract with exchange
uasx.description: Swaps the halves of Rm, then puts Rn.hi + Rm.lo in the top halfword and Rn.lo - Rm.hi in the bottom one, unsigned and wrapping; GE bits record the carry of the sum and the no-borrow of the difference. Used for complex-number style arithmetic in DSP code.

ubfx.description: Pulls a field of width bits starting at bit lsb out of Rn and right-aligns it in Rd with zeros above. Compilers use it for bit-field struct members and for (x >> n) & mask in one instruction.

udf.description: Always raises an undefined-instruction exception; the immediate (16 bits in A32 and 32-bit Thumb, 8 bits in 16-bit Thumb) is ignored by the CPU but can carry a code. Compilers emit it for traps and unreachable code; LLVM prints the __builtin_trap encoding as trap.

udiv.description: Divides Rn by Rm as unsigned 32-bit integers, rounding toward zero; dividing by zero gives 0. Present on armv8 and on armv7 cores with the divide extension; otherwise compilers call __aeabi_uidiv, so seeing udiv tells you the target CPU has it.

uhadd16.description: Adds the two unsigned halfwords of Rn and Rm lane by lane and halves each sum, keeping the carry bit so nothing overflows. Used in DSP and image code for averaging pairs of 16-bit values; GE flags are not touched.

uhadd8.description: Adds the four unsigned bytes of Rn and Rm lane by lane and halves each sum without losing the carry. Image code uses it to average pixels four at a time; GE flags are not touched.

uhasx.summary: Unsigned halving add and subtract with exchange
uhasx.description: Like UASX, it computes Rn.hi + Rm.lo for the top halfword and Rn.lo - Rm.hi for the bottom one, but halves both results so they always fit. GE flags are not touched; found only in hand-tuned DSP code.

uhsax.summary: Unsigned halving subtract and add with exchange
uhsax.description: Computes Rn.hi - Rm.lo for the top halfword and Rn.lo + Rm.hi for the bottom one, unsigned, halving both results so they always fit. GE flags are not touched; it belongs to hand-tuned DSP code.

uhsub16.description: Subtracts the unsigned halfwords of Rm from those of Rn lane by lane and halves each difference, keeping the borrow so the result is exact. Used in DSP code; GE flags are not touched.

uhsub8.description: Subtracts the four unsigned bytes of Rm from those of Rn lane by lane and halves each difference, keeping the borrow so the result is exact. Used in hand-written image and DSP code; GE flags are not touched.

umaal.description: Multiplies Rn by Rm as unsigned 32-bit values into a 64-bit product and adds both RdLo and RdHi to it as separate 32-bit numbers, writing the 64-bit result back to RdHi:RdLo; it can never overflow. Big-number code such as OpenSSL/BoringSSL uses it for multiprecision multiplication.

umlal.description: Multiplies Rn by Rm as unsigned 32-bit values and adds the 64-bit product to the 64-bit value held in RdHi:RdLo. Compilers use it for uint64_t multiply-add and in 64-bit multiplication sequences.

umlals.summary: Unsigned multiply accumulate long, setting flags
umlals.description: The A32 flag-setting form of UMLAL: accumulates the unsigned 64-bit product of Rn and Rm into RdHi:RdLo and sets N and Z from the 64-bit result, leaving C and V unchanged. Rare in compiled code.

umull.description: Multiplies Rn by Rm as unsigned 32-bit values and writes the full 64-bit product to RdHi:RdLo. Compilers use it for 32x32-to-64 multiplication, as part of uint64_t multiplication, and to divide by a constant via the high word of a multiply by a magic number.

umulls.description: The A32 flag-setting form of UMULL: writes the unsigned 64-bit product of Rn and Rm to RdHi:RdLo and sets N and Z from it, leaving C and V unchanged. Rare in compiled code.

uqadd16.description: Adds the two unsigned halfwords of Rn and Rm lane by lane, clamping each sum at 0xFFFF instead of wrapping. Neither Q nor GE is changed; DSP and audio code uses it.

uqadd8.description: Adds the four unsigned bytes of Rn and Rm lane by lane, clamping each sum at 255 instead of wrapping. Neither Q nor GE is changed; image code uses it to brighten or blend pixels without overflow.

uqasx.summary: Unsigned saturating add and subtract with exchange
uqasx.description: Computes Rn.hi + Rm.lo for the top halfword and Rn.lo - Rm.hi for the bottom one, clamping each unsigned result to 0–0xFFFF. Neither Q nor GE is changed; it appears in hand-tuned DSP code.
uqasx.operation: Rd.H[1] = sat_u16(Rn.H[1] + Rm.H[0]); Rd.H[0] = sat_u16(Rn.H[0] - Rm.H[1])

uqsax.summary: Unsigned saturating subtract and add with exchange
uqsax.description: Computes Rn.hi - Rm.lo for the top halfword and Rn.lo + Rm.hi for the bottom one, clamping each unsigned result to 0–0xFFFF. Neither Q nor GE is changed; it appears in hand-tuned DSP code.
uqsax.operation: Rd.H[1] = sat_u16(Rn.H[1] - Rm.H[0]); Rd.H[0] = sat_u16(Rn.H[0] + Rm.H[1])

uqsub16.description: Subtracts the unsigned halfwords of Rm from those of Rn lane by lane, clamping each result at 0 instead of wrapping. Neither Q nor GE is changed; used in DSP code.

uqsub8.description: Subtracts the four unsigned bytes of Rm from those of Rn lane by lane, clamping each result at 0 instead of wrapping. Neither Q nor GE is changed; image code uses it for darkening pixels or byte-wise max/min tricks.

usad8.description: Takes the absolute difference of each of the four unsigned byte pairs in Rn and Rm and adds the four results into one 32-bit value. Video encoders use it for block matching, and it also gives a quick byte-wise distance between two words.

usada8.summary: Unsigned sum of absolute differences and accumulate
usada8.description: Like USAD8, sums the absolute differences of the four unsigned byte pairs in Rn and Rm, then adds that sum to Ra. Video encoders use it in loops that accumulate the difference between two pixel blocks.

usat.description: Optionally shifts Rn left or arithmetically right, then clamps the signed result to the unsigned range 0 to 2^imm - 1, setting the Q flag if it had to clamp. Compilers and image code use it to clamp values to 0–255 for pixels.

usat16.description: Treats each halfword of Rn as a signed 16-bit value and clamps it to the unsigned range 0 to 2^imm - 1 (imm up to 15), setting Q if any lane was clamped. DSP code uses it to bring two intermediate results back into pixel or sample range.

usax.summary: Unsigned subtract and add with exchange
usax.description: Swaps the halves of Rm, then puts Rn.hi - Rm.lo in the top halfword and Rn.lo + Rm.hi in the bottom one, unsigned and wrapping; GE bits record the no-borrow of the difference and the carry of the sum. Used in hand-tuned DSP code.

usub16.description: Subtracts the unsigned halfwords of Rm from those of Rn lane by lane, wrapping around, and sets each pair of GE bits when its lane did not borrow (Rn.H >= Rm.H). Followed by SEL it gives a per-lane unsigned maximum or minimum.

usub8.description: Subtracts the four unsigned bytes of Rm from those of Rn lane by lane, wrapping around, and sets a GE bit for each byte that did not borrow. Combined with SEL it gives a byte-wise unsigned maximum or minimum, as in hand-written image code.

uxtab.description: Takes the low byte of Rm (optionally rotated right by 8, 16 or 24 first), zero-extends it and adds it to Rn. Compilers fold an unsigned char widening into an addition or table index with it.

uxtab16.summary: Zero-extend two bytes and add halfwords
uxtab16.description: Picks bytes 0 and 2 of Rm (after an optional rotation by 8, 16 or 24), zero-extends each to 16 bits and adds them to the two halfwords of Rn separately. DSP and pixel code uses it to accumulate unsigned 8-bit values in 16-bit lanes.

uxtah.description: Zero-extends the low halfword of Rm (optionally rotated right by 8, 16 or 24 first) and adds it to Rn. Compilers use it to fold an unsigned short widening into an addition or an address calculation.

uxtb.description: Keeps only the low 8 bits of Rm (optionally after rotating it right by 8, 16 or 24), clearing the rest. Compilers emit it for unsigned char and bool conversions and for x & 0xff; with a rotation it extracts byte 1, 2 or 3.

uxtb16.description: Zero-extends bytes 0 and 2 of Rm (after an optional rotation by 8, 16 or 24) into the two 16-bit halves of Rd, which is the same as masking with 0x00FF00FF. Compilers use it for that mask, and pixel code to split RGBA channels into halfword lanes.

uxth.description: Keeps only the low 16 bits of Rm (optionally after rotating it right by 8, 16 or 24), clearing the rest. Compilers emit it for unsigned short and uint16_t conversions and for x & 0xffff.

vaba.description: For each lane of two D or Q registers, takes the absolute difference of the signed or unsigned 8-, 16- or 32-bit integers and adds it into the destination lane. NEON code for motion estimation and image comparison uses it to accumulate sums of absolute differences.

vabal.summary: Vector absolute difference and accumulate long
vabal.description: Takes the absolute differences of the signed or unsigned integer lanes of two D registers and adds them into a Q register whose lanes are twice as wide, so the sums do not overflow. Used in NEON sum-of-absolute-differences loops over 8-bit pixels.

vabd.description: Writes the absolute difference of each pair of lanes from two D or Q registers, for signed or unsigned 8-, 16- or 32-bit integers or for floats (f16, f32). Compilers emit it for vectorized abs(a - b), and NEON intrinsics code uses it for distances and error metrics.

vabdl.description: Takes the absolute differences of the signed or unsigned integer lanes of two D registers and writes them into a Q register with lanes of twice the width. NEON image code uses it as the first step of sum-of-absolute-differences computations.

vabs.description: Writes the absolute value of a scalar float (vabs.f32 Sd, vabs.f64 Dd, also f16) or of every lane of a D or Q register (s8, s16, s32 or float). Compilers use the scalar form for fabs/fabsf; the integer vector form wraps for the most negative value instead of saturating.

vacge.summary: Vector FP absolute compare greater or equal
vacge.description: Compares the absolute values of float lanes (f32 or f16) and sets each destination lane to all ones when |Dn| >= |Dm| and to zero otherwise. The assembler alias VACLE is the same with the operands swapped; NEON code uses the mask for range checks.

vacgt.summary: Vector FP absolute compare greater than
vacgt.description: Compares the absolute values of float lanes (f32 or f16) and sets each destination lane to all ones when |Dn| > |Dm| and to zero otherwise. The assembler alias VACLT is the same with the operands swapped.

vacle.summary: Vector FP absolute compare less or equal (= VACGE)
vacle.description: An assembler alias of VACGE with the source operands swapped: each lane becomes all ones when |Dn| <= |Dm|. Disassemblers print the underlying vacge with reversed operands instead.

vaclt.summary: Vector FP absolute compare less than (= VACGT)
vaclt.description: An assembler alias of VACGT with the source operands swapped: each lane becomes all ones when |Dn| < |Dm|. Disassemblers print the underlying vacgt with reversed operands instead.

vadd.description: Adds two scalar floats (vadd.f32 Sd, vadd.f64 Dd, also f16), or every lane of two D or Q registers as integers (i8 to i64, wrapping) or floats. The scalar form is what compilers emit for float and double addition; the vector forms come from auto-vectorized loops and NEON intrinsics.
vadd.operation: Dd = Dn + Dm  (per lane for vectors)

vaddhn.summary: Vector add and narrow, high half
vaddhn.description: Adds the 16-, 32- or 64-bit lanes of two Q registers and keeps only the upper half of each sum, producing a D register of half-width lanes. NEON code uses it for fixed-point arithmetic where only the high part of the result matters.

vaddl.description: Adds the signed or unsigned 8-, 16- or 32-bit lanes of two D registers and writes the sums into a Q register with lanes of twice the width, so nothing overflows. Compilers emit it when vectorizing sums of narrow types, such as adding uint8_t pixels into 16-bit totals.

vaddw.description: Widens each signed or unsigned lane of a D register to twice its width and adds it to the matching lane of a Q register. Vectorized loops use it to accumulate narrow values into wide running totals.

vand.description: ANDs two D or Q registers bit by bit; the element type suffix is ignored. vand with an immediate is an assembler alias of VBIC with the inverted constant. NEON code uses it to apply masks, for example the result of a vector compare.

vbic.description: Clears in the destination every bit set in the second operand: either another D or Q register (Dn AND NOT Dm) or an immediate replicated into each 16- or 32-bit lane. NEON code uses it to apply inverted masks and to clear fields in all lanes at once.

vbif.description: Copies bits of Dn into the destination wherever the matching bit of Dm is 0, keeping the destination's own bits where Dm is 1. One of the three bitwise selects compilers choose between to implement a vector ternary after a compare.

vbit.description: Copies bits of Dn into the destination wherever the matching bit of Dm is 1, keeping the destination's own bits where Dm is 0. Compilers use it, like VBSL and VBIF, to blend two vectors under a compare mask.

vbsl.description: Uses the destination as a mask: takes bits from Dn where the mask bit is 1 and from Dm where it is 0. Compilers emit it for vectorized a ? b : c and for copysign, typically right after a VCEQ/VCGT that built the mask.

vcadd.description: Treats adjacent pairs of float lanes (f16 or f32) as complex numbers and adds Dn to Dm rotated by 90 or 270 degrees, which amounts to adding or subtracting the swapped real and imaginary parts. Part of the Armv8.3 complex-number extension; unconditional.

vceq.description: Compares each pair of lanes for equality, as integers (i8, i16, i32) or floats, or each lane against zero, and sets the destination lane to all ones when equal and zero otherwise. Vectorized code uses the mask with VBSL or VAND.

vcge.description: Sets each destination lane to all ones when the lane of Dn is greater than or equal to that of Dm (signed, unsigned or float), or compares against zero, and to zero otherwise. The register form of VCLE is this with the operands swapped.

vcgt.description: Sets each destination lane to all ones when the lane of Dn is greater than that of Dm (signed, unsigned or float), or greater than zero, and to zero otherwise. The register form of VCLT is this with the operands swapped; compilers use the mask for vector max, min and selects.

vcle.description: Sets each lane to all ones when the signed or float lane of Dm is less than or equal to zero, and to zero otherwise. The two-register form is an assembler alias of VCGE with the operands swapped, so disassemblers print vcge for it.

vcls.description: Counts, in each signed 8-, 16- or 32-bit lane, how many bits after the top one are equal to it, which tells how far the value can be shifted left without overflow. Fixed-point NEON code uses it to normalize values.

vclt.description: Sets each lane to all ones when the signed or float lane of Dm is less than zero, and to zero otherwise; a quick way to build a sign mask. The two-register form is an assembler alias of VCGT with the operands swapped, so disassemblers print vcgt for it.
